title: Uesugi Kenshin Sends Salt to His Enemy
text:
In 16th century Japan, Uesugi Kenshin and Takeda Shingen were the most famous rivals of the Warring States period. They fought each other again and again at Kawanakajima without either winning a final victory.

According to a tradition recorded in the Edo period, around 1567 or 1568 the Imagawa and Hojo clans, who had turned against Takeda, cut off the supply of salt to his mountain province of Kai. Kai had no coast, and without salt its people would suffer. Kenshin's province of Echigo lay on the sea. He was urged to join the blockade and weaken his great enemy.

Kenshin refused. In the story he declares that he fights Shingen with bows and swords, not with rice and salt, and he allowed salt to flow to Kai at fair prices. Some versions add that Shingen sent him a fine sword in thanks.

The tale gave Japanese the expression "sending salt to the enemy," still used for helping a rival in trouble. When Shingen died in 1573, Kenshin is said to have wept for the loss of so worthy an opponent.
lesson: Compete hard with your rivals, but do not win by making innocent people suffer. How you fight says as much about you as whether you win.
location: Echigo and Kai provinces (modern Niigata and Yamanashi, Japan)
source: Edo-period tradition and later popular histories of the Sengoku period
caveat: The episode is not attested in contemporary documents and is generally treated as legend.
